title: The Butter Forecast

beats.text: The best stock market forecast ever found ran on butter.
Imagine a quant slides you one chart.
Butter production in Bangladesh explained seventy-five percent of the stock market's moves.
Add American cheese, and the lines got even tighter.
Then he threw in sheep, Bangladeshi and American, every last one.
Ninety-nine percent. A near-perfect forecast from a farmyard.
So why isn't every fund on earth watching cows?
Because outside the years he tested, the magic died.
You see, it's like your lucky socks.
Wear them to enough games, and some day your team wins anyway.
He'd dug through a United Nations database and kept whatever fit the past.
Search enough numbers, and pure chance hands you a perfect match.
The whole thing was a joke, built to warn investors.
And investors still called him, asking for the latest butter numbers.

facts.claim: In David Leinweber's data-mining demonstration, annual butter production in Bangladesh 'explained' 75% of the variation in the S&P 500 (R-squared 0.75)
Adding US cheese production (and US butter) raised the fit to about 95%, then adding the sheep population of Bangladesh and the US raised it to 99%

The relationship was useless outside the fitted period ('a total crock before 1983 or after 1993' / 'useless as a predictor before 1983 or after 1999'); sources differ on the exact years, so the narration names none
The data series were mined from a United Nations database (CD-ROM) of international economic data
It was intended as a joke / tongue-in-cheek warning about data mining and overfitting in quantitative investing
Investors and money managers later contacted him asking for the latest Bangladeshi butter production numbers
Leinweber is not named or depicted (living person); he is referred to only as 'a quant'

caption:
Butter production in Bangladesh once 'explained' 75% of the S&P 500. Add cheese and sheep: 99%.
It was a joke about data mining, and it only worked on the past. Investors still asked for the butter numbers.
